data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious goal, whereas Popper's methodology is deliberately aimed at truth-seeking.","Organisms do not 'prefer' other organisms; scientists actively choose theories.","Evolutionary fitness is reproductive success; corroboration is logical resilience."],"overturn_conditions":["If biological fitness actually implied a probabilistic guarantee of future survival.","If scientists chose theories randomly rather than by test severity."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of stress tests rather than prediction of future stability.","Distinction between 'fitness for current environment' and 'guarantee of future survival'.","Procedural rule vs. evidential warrant."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_003"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we cannot infer an organism will survive a new predator because it survived old ones, we cannot infer a theory is true because it passed old tests.","Preference for the 'fittest' organism is a description of nature, not a rational justification for betting on its immortality; similarly for theories."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive methodological rule aimed at maximizing falsifiability (testability), not probability; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any rational assurance that the preferred theory is true or will survive future tests, reducing scientific progress to a game of surviving increasingly severe attempts at refutation without cumulative epistemic gain.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'severity of test' implicitly assumes nature's uniformity (that what worked before will work again), the distinction collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists act on corroborated theories expecting them to work (pragmatic success), they are functionally relying on inductive inference regardless of Popper's semantic labeling.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the goal is merely 'keeping the game going' rather than approaching truth, the defense fails to explain why scientists reject falsified theories in favor of unfalsified ones for practical application.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'corroboration' (a report on past test performance) and 'probability' (a prediction of future truth). Popper argues we prefer highly corroborated theories not because they are likely true (induction), but because they have withstood the most severe tests, meaning they possess high empirical content and falsifiability. Choosing them keeps the game of science going by targeting the most vulnerable points in our knowledge. The preference is a procedural rule to maximize learning potential, not an evidential warrant for truth.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
